newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, breaking winning streak.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, breaking winning streak.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices closed lower on Wednesday to end a four-day winning streak as participants looked forward to the Friday release of the May U.S. employment report.

Prices opened lower after weakening overnight and dipped again at mid-morning. Short-covering erased the market's losses by early afternoon, pushing prices up to Tuesday's closing levels. But weakness reemerged and prices ended lower.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond closed at 96-24/32, down 5/32 to yield 6.88 percent.
The two-year note slipped 1/32 to 100-3/32, its yield closing at 6.20 percent.

"We're range-trading before Friday's payroll numbers," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "There were some day trades. People were watching the pricing of some corporate and global bond issues, but there really was not a lot going on."
At mid-morning, the market learned that factory orders rose 1.2 percent in April, a little more than expected. But the rise came after a revised 1.3 percent decline in March.
William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Co., said the market was likely to be range-bound until Friday when the Labor Department releases U.S. employment data for May.
Hornbarger said the benchmark 30-year bond yield has not broken out of the range between 6.81 percent and 7.17 percent that it has traded in since March.
"We've cycled back and forth a couple of times and now we've run it right back down toward the bottom of the range," he said. That range will hold until Friday, he said.
Economists polled by Reuters on Monday estimated on average that 219,000 new jobs were added to non-farm payrolls in May.

Analysts said May payroll growth of 125,000 new jobs could push the 30-year bond price up more than a point. A number near consensus would leave the bond unchanged. Payroll growth of more than 300,000 jobs would send bond prices down sharply.
Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi, said Friday's payrolls data "could change the picture that is evolving of this being a stronger market."
"We're constantly changing our expectations," said Rupkey.

Seasonal adjustment factors are expected to depress the May payroll growth to be reported on Friday. That means that even a very moderate payroll growth number could be explained away and discounted by the market as attributable to the peculiarities of the seasonal adjustments, analysts said.
Other items in the employment data could also affect the bond market's reaction to the May report.
"The workweek length will be important to look at," said Youngdahl. "We expect hourly earnings to be up 0.3 percent. Factory overtime hours will also be looked at."
The 10-year Treasury note ended at 100-1/32, down 1/32, its yield at 6.62 percent. Five-year Treasury notes ended at 100-2/32, down 2/32, to yield 6.49 percent.
Three-month bill rates ended at 4.94 percent, six-month rates ended at 5.18 percent and year bill rates closed at 5.45 percent.
